title: Relative Enthalpies Can Be Determined from Heat Capacity Data and Heats of Transition
lead: Warming ice from −20 °C to liquid water at +20 °C takes three steps, and each has its own enthalpy change. Differential scanning calorimetry measures the heat capacity behind them as a sample is heated.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page; its unnumbered DSC image is folded into Figure 19.10.1.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercises for this section; the one here is new and AI-written, its answer checked by computation from the values the question gives. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: Schematic enthalpy function showing the jump at the melting point. The ideal heat capacity signal and its broadened DSC signal

exercises.source_id: The total change in enthalpy between -20 and +20 would be the sum of the three enthalpy changes.
exercises.prompt: Take $C_{P,\text{ice}} = 37.7$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, $C_{P,\text{water}} = 75.29$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $\kDeltafusH = 6.01$ kJ/mol at 273 K, each constant. Find the enthalpy change, in kJ/mol, for taking ice at −20 °C to liquid water at +20 °C.

answer.hint: Define the process: heat the ice, melt it, heat the water.
answer.solution: $\kDeltaH_1 = (37.7)(273 - 253) = 754$ J/mol to warm the ice, $\kDeltafusH = 6010$ J/mol to melt it, and $\kDeltaH_3 = (75.29)(293 - 273) = 1506$ J/mol to warm the water. The sum is $754 + 6010 + 1506 = 8270$ J/mol, or 8.27 kJ/mol. Melting accounts for almost three quarters of it.

footnotes.html: Figure 19.10.1 shows one transition, melting. Boiling would add a second jump in $H$ and a second singularity in $C_p$.
